title: APRA urges banks to bolster AI risk controls, not slow down deployment
full_text:
Artificial intelligence is accelerating at such a rapid pace that financial services players have no choice but to adopt it broadly and improve governance along the way, the prudential regulator says, as it backs a new industry blueprint to improve the management of emerging risks.
“It is easy for a regulator to say, ‘Just slow down and stop [and] get these things in place before you start operating’,” the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority’s top banking regulator Therese McCarthy Hockey said. “Actually, you just don’t have that luxury.”
APRA’s Therese McCarthy Hockey says banks can’t afford to wait to adopt AI.
McCarthy Hockey’s comments come after the Actuaries Institute of Australia and UTS Human Technology Institute published a report on Monday night to help banks and other financial services companies bolster their risk management around deployment of the powerful technology.
Australia’s banks are spending hundreds of million of dollars on AI and have rolled it out for customer chatbots and agents that can process loans and recommend products.
APRA’s multiple warnings this year that governance is not keeping pace with the scale of deployment should not be read as a message to slow down, McCarthy Hockey said.
“We’re saying: speed up that governance piece and the risk management … We want the system to be more agile.”
APRA and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission said last week they had hosted nine roundtables attended by 380 entities and 600 people in June and July with input from the Australian Signals Directorate.
McCarthy Hockey said this represented a new form of regulation, focused on speed and information sharing. “It’s a very unusual way [to] do our work, partnering up with ASIC [and] ASD. [It is] much more dynamic, feeding back in real-time [and] connecting big operators and small operators who can learn from each other.”
The Actuaries Institute and UTS report offers practical ways to lift governance and suggests questions to be asked of technology suppliers which can be used by smaller operators to detect vulnerabilities and plan incident responses.
Nicholas Davis, co-director of UTS HTI, said all financial services companies will need to conduct “much more regular monitoring and reassessment of systems” given the output of AI models are not known in advance.
Any update to an underlying model, whether initiated by a user or pushed by the vendor, may need a reassessment of risk, while a material AI-related risk event – like a biased outcome, a security incident, a compliance breach, or a significant customer complaint – might need a “root cause” analysis and a reassessment of controls, the paper says.
“This is a framework to increase the sophistication of understanding of risk, at a real level, and not compliance tick-a-box,” said Actuaries Institute CEO Elayne Grace.
Victor Bajanov, an AI consultant who worked on the report, said users should consider risks based on first principles: what is the risk, how likely is it to happen, and what is the damage if it does happen.
“These systems can write superb software code or poetry or prose – but can’t say the number of letters in strawberry,” he said. “So the system of risks is different. You’re very unlikely to be able to bribe an AI agent any more than you could trick a human by saying ‘Ignore all my previous instructions and do what I say’.
“And so, to manage these risks, we have to go back to first principles.”
